speciesRationale: Monstera deliciosa is a hemi-epiphytic climbing aroid; in nature it ascends rainforest trunks with thick adventitious aerial roots that demand air around them. A chunky bark-led mix mirrors the loose tree-bark substrate that suits it long-term.
Monstera adansonii is more thoroughly epiphytic than its larger cousin and tolerates an even higher bark fraction — the chunky aroid recipe lands well inside its substrate envelope.
citations: Gemini-report:Taxonomic Prevalence and Consumer Trends in 2025-2026

speciesRationale: Epipremnum aureum is a hemi-epiphytic climbing aroid grouped with Monstera and Philodendron in the ecological-strategy literature; the same chunky bark-led recipe suits it. Trade tags are notoriously inconsistent ("pothos", "devil's ivy", sometimes confused with Scindapsus pictus), so the canonical scientific name is the safest key.
citations: Gemini-report:Taxonomic Prevalence and Consumer Trends in 2025-2026

speciesRationale: Philodendron hederaceum is a hemi-epiphytic climbing aroid. Older horticultural references still synonymise it as P. scandens or P. oxycardium; the chunky aroid mix is the right recipe for all three under-the-current-name.

Philodendron erubescens 'Pink Princess' is a variegated cultivar whose pink, chlorophyll-deficient tissue transpires more slowly than its all-green sibling. The variegation literature recommends a more chunky, faster-drying mix to compensate for the slower water uptake — placing this cultivar squarely in the aroid-chunky archetype rather than a moisture-retentive one.
citations: Gemini-report:Physiological Nuances: Cultivars and Variegation Management

speciesRationale: Spathiphyllum wallisii is a terrestrial aroid native to the tropical Americas; the houseplant care literature groups it with the moisture-loving terrestrials and notes it tolerates boggy conditions without being truly aquatic. A coir-led, sphagnum-amended mix keeps its fibrous root system evenly moist.

Ficus lyrata is a terrestrial fig with a fibrous root system; despite sharing a genus with the rubber plant it sits at the drier end of Ficus moisture tolerance. The standard coir-perlite-bark mix gives the even drainage it needs without the moisture-retention that suits its tropical-rainforest relatives.
citations: Gemini-report:Taxonomic Prevalence and Consumer Trends in 2025-2026

speciesRationale: Ficus elastica shares the fibrous, terrestrial root profile of its genus and the same standard houseplant substrate envelope. The literature flags watering cadence — not substrate archetype — as the per-species variable inside Ficus.

Dracaena trifasciata (formerly Sansevieria trifasciata) is a stem-succulent grouped with the xerophytic taxa; the Byng et al. 2018 transfer into Dracaena is not yet reflected on most retail tags, so the Sansevieria name persists as an alias. A gritty mineral-led mix is required because saturated organic media rots its thick fleshy leaves at the base.

Zamioculcas zamiifolia is a drought-adapted aroid that stores water in tuberous rhizomes; the brief lists it in the water-storing-tuberous-roots group. Despite its taxonomic home in Araceae, it sits with the succulents for substrate purposes — a gritty mineral mix avoids rotting the rhizome between waterings.
citations: Gemini-report:Taxonomic Prevalence and Consumer Trends in 2025-2026

speciesRationale: Chlorophytum comosum is a terrestrial monocot with thickened storage roots; the ecological-strategy literature groups it with the standard terrestrials, and the retail-trends data notes it as a revived 1970s favourite carrying significant volume. A coir-led standard mix matches its moderate-moisture preference.
citations: Gemini-report:Taxonomic Prevalence and Consumer Trends in 2025-2026

speciesRationale: Phalaenopsis is modelled at the genus rank because retail moth-orchids are uniformly hybrid grex plants with effectively indistinguishable substrate needs; species-level resolution adds no signal. Its velamen-coated aerial roots are evolved for fast wet-dry cycling on tree branches, so a coarse bark-charcoal-perlite epiphytic mix replicates the habitat.

Goeppertia orbifolia (transferred from Calathea by Borchsenius and corroborated in POWO) is a humidity-sensitive terrestrial that punishes substrate dry-back; the moisture-retentive coir-bark-sphagnum recipe holds the even moisture it requires. The Calathea name persists on retail tags and is carried as an alias.
citations: Gemini-report:Taxonomic Prevalence and Consumer Trends in 2025-2026

speciesRationale: Crassula ovata is a classic Crassulaceae succulent with thick water-storing leaves and a CAM photosynthetic pathway. A gritty mineral-led mix is required; the houseplant-trade name confusion around "jade plant", "money tree", and "lucky bamboo" makes the canonical binomial the only reliable database key.

Saintpaulia ionantha is a calcifuge that loses micronutrient access above pH 6.5; the ericaceous low-pH recipe is the only archetype in the corpus that defends the pH 4.5–5.5 band the species requires. This archetype was added to the v1 set specifically to support Saintpaulia per the GEMINI cross-critique.

Hoya carnosa is lithophytic / semi-terrestrial — neither purely epiphytic nor purely xerophytic. The literature documents real substrate-needs tension within the genus between predominantly epiphytic species (most Hoya, including H. carnosa) and the more terrestrial outliers. A 60/40 blend of aroid-chunky and succulent-gritty captures the airflow Hoya carnosa wants while keeping the mineral fraction high enough to dry between waterings.

Aglaonema is a terrestrial-to-hemi-epiphytic aroid (Araceae) that shares the chunky-aroid substrate envelope with Monstera and Philodendron: its roots want high air-filled porosity and resent the compaction of a peat-perlite mix. Modelled at genus rank — retail 'Chinese evergreen' spans many hybrids with effectively identical substrate needs. Mildly toxic: the foliage carries insoluble calcium-oxalate crystals (raphides) that irritate mouth and throat if chewed, so keep clippings away from pets and children.
citations: Drafter-sourced horticulture (Araceae chunky-aroid substrate; calcium-oxalate toxicity)

speciesRationale: Alocasia (elephant ear) is a tuberous tropical aroid that grows in loose, fast-draining forest-floor litter; the chunky bark-led aroid mix matches its preference for moisture with abundant air around the rhizome and rejects the waterlogging that rots its tuber. Modelled at genus rank across the many commercial hybrids. Toxic: high in insoluble calcium oxalate — ingestion causes intense oral and gastrointestinal irritation in pets and humans, so site it out of reach and handle sap with care.
citations: Drafter-sourced horticulture (Alocasia tuber/aroid substrate; calcium-oxalate toxicity)

speciesRationale: Anthurium andraeanum (flamingo flower) is an epiphytic/hemi-epiphytic aroid whose thick aerial-leaning roots demand the open, bark-dominant structure of the chunky aroid mix; in a dense mix it suffers root rot. Mildly toxic: like other aroids it contains insoluble calcium-oxalate raphides that irritate the mouth if chewed — keep away from pets and children.
citations: Drafter-sourced horticulture (Anthurium epiphytic aroid substrate; calcium-oxalate toxicity)

speciesRationale: Dieffenbachia (dumb cane) is a terrestrial aroid that thrives in the loose, airy, bark-led substrate of the chunky aroid archetype; its fleshy stem base rots in a compacted, water-retentive mix. Modelled at genus rank across common cultivars. Toxic — the common name 'dumb cane' names the hazard: the sap is laden with insoluble calcium-oxalate raphides plus proteolytic enzymes that, if chewed, cause painful swelling of the mouth, tongue and throat and temporary loss of speech. Keep strictly away from pets and children; wear gloves when pruning and wash hands afterwards.
citations: Drafter-sourced toxicity reference (insoluble calcium oxalate; oral swelling, 'dumb cane' effect)

speciesRationale: Aloe vera is a leaf-succulent (Asphodelaceae) that stores water in thick gel-filled leaves and evolved in arid, mineral, free-draining ground. The gritty mineral-led mix is essential: in moisture-retentive media the stem base and roots rot quickly. Water only when the substrate has dried fully through.

Kalanchoe is a Crassulaceae leaf-succulent with CAM metabolism and water-storing leaves; it needs the fast-drying gritty mineral mix that protects succulents from basal rot, and flowers best kept on the dry side. Modelled at genus rank. Toxic to pets: the genus contains bufadienolide cardiac glycosides that can cause vomiting and, rarely, heart-rhythm disturbance in cats and dogs if eaten — keep out of their reach.

Maranta leuconeura (prayer plant) is a shallow-rooted tropical terrestrial that punishes substrate dry-back with crisping leaf edges; the coir-led moisture-retentive mix with sphagnum holds the even, steady moisture it requires without becoming waterlogged. Non-toxic to cats and dogs, a safe choice for pet households.
citations: Drafter-sourced horticulture (Maranta dry-back-intolerant terrestrial; moisture-retentive substrate)

speciesRationale: Nephrolepis exaltata (Boston fern) is a moisture-loving terrestrial fern with fine fibrous roots that desiccate rapidly; the coir-and-sphagnum moisture-retentive mix buffers the constant dampness it needs. A dedicated fern archetype was considered and rejected as redundant — the moisture-retentive substrate envelope already covers it. Non-toxic to pets and humans.
citations: Drafter-sourced horticulture (Nephrolepis moisture-loving fern; moisture-retentive substrate)

speciesRationale: Pachira aquatica (money tree) is a wetland-margin tree that, indoors, does best in a free-draining standard coir-perlite-bark mix that stays evenly moist but never sodden — despite its swampy origins, container culture rots its roots if the mix holds water. Non-toxic to pets and people. The 'money tree' trade name is shared with the unrelated jade plant (Crassula ovata), so the binomial is the reliable key.

Dypsis lutescens (areca / golden cane palm) is a clumping palm with fine, brittle roots that want a free-draining yet moisture-holding medium; the standard coir-perlite-bark mix covers its peat-based, well-aerated substrate envelope for indoor culture. A dedicated palm archetype was considered and rejected as redundant for this sprint. Non-toxic to pets and humans.

This entry covers the standard tree-form Dracaena species (notably D. marginata and D. fragrans) grown for foliage — distinct from the succulent snake plant Dracaena trifasciata, which keeps its own gritty-mineral mapping. These dracaenas are fibrous-rooted terrestrials suited to the standard coir-perlite-bark mix; they are sensitive to fluoride and salt build-up, so a free-draining mix that flushes easily helps. Modelled at genus rank. Mildly toxic to cats and dogs (saponins) — ingestion can cause vomiting and drooling; keep away from pets.
citations: Drafter-sourced horticulture (tree-form Dracaena standard substrate; fluoride sensitivity)

speciesRationale: Tradescantia (spiderwort / inch plant) is a fast-growing trailing terrestrial that roots readily and tolerates a broad moisture range; the standard coir-perlite-bark mix suits its vigorous fibrous roots. Modelled at genus rank. Mild irritant: the sap can cause contact dermatitis on sensitive skin and is mildly irritating to pets if chewed — handle cuttings with light care.

Hedera helix (English ivy) is a woody evergreen climber that, indoors, thrives in a free-draining standard coir-perlite-bark mix kept lightly moist. Toxic to both pets and humans: leaves and berries contain triterpenoid saponins (hederagenin) that cause gastrointestinal upset if eaten, and the sap is a known contact-dermatitis allergen — wear gloves when pruning and keep it away from pets and children.
citations: Drafter-sourced toxicity reference (triterpenoid saponins; contact dermatitis)

speciesRationale: Schefflera (umbrella tree) is a woody tropical that grows vigorously in a standard well-draining coir-perlite-bark mix kept evenly moist. Modelled at genus rank (S. arboricola and S. actinophylla). Toxic: the foliage contains insoluble calcium-oxalate crystals that irritate the mouth and gut of pets and humans if chewed — keep out of reach of cats, dogs and children.

Euphorbia pulcherrima (poinsettia) is grown as a short-lived flowering houseplant; a free-draining standard coir-perlite-bark mix kept lightly moist (never waterlogged) is correct — its roots rot fast in sodden media. Irritant/latex: like all Euphorbia it exudes a milky latex sap that irritates skin and eyes and causes mild mouth and stomach upset if eaten. Its toxicity is widely overstated, but the latex is a genuine irritant, so wash hands after handling and keep cuttings from pets and children.
citations: Drafter-sourced toxicity reference (Euphorbia latex irritant; toxicity overstated)

speciesRationale: Dionaea muscipula (Venus flytrap) is a temperate carnivorous bog plant and the sole species needing the carnivorous-peat-sand archetype: a nutrient-poor 50/50 sphagnum-peat and lime-free silica-sand mix. Its care is unlike any other houseplant — water ONLY with distilled, reverse-osmosis or rainwater (tap-water minerals are lethal over time), give it NO fertiliser (it feeds by trapping insects) and NO lime or dolomite, keep the medium permanently damp in bright direct light, and respect its winter dormancy (a cool rest of several weeks). Non-toxic, but avoid triggering the traps for amusement — each trap closes only a limited number of times.
citations: Drafter-sourced horticulture (carnivorous bog mix; distilled-water/no-fertiliser/no-lime mandate; dormancy)
